label: weak solution
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{weak solution}A vector field $u: [0,T) \times \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a weak solution to \eqref{E} with initial data $u(0)=u_0:\mathbb{R}^2  \to \mathbb{R}^2$ if 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $u \in L^2_{loc}([0,T)\times \mathbb{R}^2)$,\\
\item 
$$
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \Bigl\{ u\cdot\partial_t\phi + u_ku_l\partial_{x_l}\phi_k\Bigr\}\,dx\,dt = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} u_0\cdot\phi(0)\,dx
$$
for all $\phi \in C_c^{\infty}([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^2)$ with $\text{div }\phi=0$, where we sum over repeated indices, and
\item For each $t \in [0,T)$, $\text{div }u=0$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$.
\end{enumerate}

label: admissible theta
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{admissible theta} We say that the function $\theta:[1,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^+$ is admissible if 
    $$
    \int_0^1 \frac{ds}{\beta_{M,\phi}(s)}=\infty,
    $$
    where $\phi(p)=p\theta(p)$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $\theta:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)$ be non-decreasing, let $\phi(p)=p\theta(p)$, and let $\beta{_{M,\phi}}$ be as in \eqref{Beta definition}. If 
$$
\int_0^1 \frac{ds}{\beta_{M,\phi}(s)}=\infty,
$$
then
$$
\int_1^{\infty} \frac{dp}{\theta(p)}=\infty.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by noting that $\beta_{M,\phi}(s)=M\beta_{1,\phi}(s/M)$, so without loss of generality we can assume that $M=1$. For the sake of contradiction, assume that 
$$
\int_1^{\infty}\frac{dp}{\theta(p)}<\infty.
$$
Since $\theta$ is non-decreasing, we see that $\frac{1}{\theta}$ is non-increasing, and hence
$$
\frac{p}{2\theta(p)} \leq \int_{p/2}^p \frac{ds}{\theta(s)} \to 0 \text{ as }p \to \infty.
$$
In particular, one has that $\frac{\theta(p)}{p} \to \infty$. Since $\theta(p) \geq 1$, there exists $C>0$ such that $\theta(p) \geq Cp$ for all $p \geq 2$. Setting $p=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\beta_{1,\phi}(s) &= \inf_{p \geq 2} \left\{s^{1-1/p}p\theta(p)\right\}\\
& \geq Cs \inf_{p \geq 2} \left\{ p^2\exp\left(\frac{\log(1/s)}{p}\right)\right\}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
For $0 <s \leq e^{-4}$, the last expression is minimized at $p=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{1}{s}\right)$ which implies $\beta_{1,\phi}(s) \geq \frac{Ce^2}{4}s(\log(1/s))^2$. It follows that 
$$
\int_0^{e^{-4}} \frac{ds}{\beta_{1,\phi}(s)} \leq \frac{4}{Ce^2}\int_0^{e^{-4}}\frac{ds}{s(\log(1/s))^2}<\infty.
$$
Moreover, we claim that $\beta_{1,\phi(s)} \geq 2s$ for $0<s \leq 1$. To see this, note that 
\begin{equation*}
\beta_{1,\phi}(s) =s\inf_{p \geq 2} s^{-1/p}p\theta(p) \geq s\inf_{p \geq 2} p\theta(p) \geq 2s,
\end{equation*}
where in the first inequality we used that $s^{-1/p} \geq 1$ and in the final inequality we used that $\theta(p) \geq 1$. It follows that the integral over $[e^{-4},1]$ is finite as well, contradicting admissibility.

label: Yudovich Uniqueness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Yudovich Uniqueness}
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded open set with $C^2$ boundary and assume that $\theta$ is an admissible function. Then for any initial data $\omega_0 \in Y^{\theta}(\Omega)$, there exists a unique weak solution of \eqref{E} such that 
$$
\omega \in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);Y^{\theta}(\Omega)), \quad u \in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);L^{\infty}(\Omega)).
$$

label: beta lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{beta lemma}
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and let $f$ and $g$ be nonnegative, measurable, real functions, such  that $f \in L^1\cap L^{\infty}(\Omega)$  and $ g \in L^{1/\varepsilon}(\Omega)$ for all $\varepsilon \in (0,1/2]$ . Let $M \geq \left\lVertf\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}$. Assume that for some positive function $\phi:[1,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^+$,
$$
\left\lVertg\right\rVert_{L^p(\Omega)} \leq \phi(p),
$$
for all $p \geq 2$. Then 
$$
\int_{\Omega} f(x)g(x)\,dx \leq \beta_{M,\phi} (\left\lVertf\right\rVert_{L^1(\Omega)}).
$$

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $1 \leq p <\infty$. We define the uniformly local $L^p$ space as
$$
L^p_{ul}(\Omega) = \left\{f \in L^p_{loc}(\Omega) : \left\lVertf\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}} = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{R}^d} \left\lVert\phi_zf\right\rVert_{L^p}<\infty\right\}.
$$
For convention we set $L^{\infty}_{ul}(\Omega)=L^{\infty}(\Omega)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: For any fixed $\lambda>0$, we can define an equivalent norm on $L^p_{ul}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ as $$\left\lVertf\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}}=\sup_{z \in \mathbb{R}^d}\left\lVert\phi_{z,\lambda}f\right\rVert_{L^p}.$$ A proof of equivalence can be found in \cite{kato1975cauchy}.

label: Gronwall
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Gronwall}
     (Gr\"onwall's Lemma) Let $T>0$ and let $L,\alpha,\beta$ be non-negative, continuous functions on $[0,T]$ with $\alpha$ nondecreasing. If for all $t\in[0,T]$, $$L(t)\leq \alpha(t)+\int_0^t \beta(s)L(s) \, ds,$$ then for all $t\in[0,T]$, $$L(t)\leq \alpha(t)\exp{\left(\int_0^t\beta(s)\,ds\right)}.$$

label: velocity gradient estimate

body_md:
\label{velocity gradient estimate}
Suppose that a divergence free $u \in L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^2))$ and $\omega = \text{curl }u \in L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{p}_{ul}(\mathbb{R}^2))$ satisfy \eqref{FLSI}.
Let $1<p<\infty$, then
$$
\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}} \leq \frac{C(d)p^2}{p-1}\left\lVert\omega(t)\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}}+C\left(\left\lVertu(t)\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}}+\left\lVertu_0\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}}\right)+Ct\sup_{0 \leq s \leq t}\left\{\left\lVertu(s)\right\rVert_{L^p_{ul}} \left\lVertu(s)\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}} \right\}.
$$

label: rate of convergence
title: Remark
body_md:
Regarding the rate of convergence in \eqref{convergence}, we obtain an analogous result to \cite{kelliher2004} and provide an overview of their result and how it relates to our result. We implicitly define the function $f:\mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ by 
$$
\int_x^{f(x)} \frac{ds}{C_3\beta_{M,\psi}(s)}=T.
$$
From the admissibility condition, we claim that $\lim_{x \to 0^+}f(x)=0$. To see this, assume for contradiction that there exists a sequence $\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ and a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x_n) \geq \delta$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then,
$$
T=\int_{x_n}^{f(x_n)} \frac{ds}{C_3\beta_{M,\psi}(s)} \geq \int_{x_n}^{\delta}\frac{ds}{C_3\beta_{M,\psi}(s)} \to \infty  \quad \text{as } n\to \infty.
$$
Hence it must be the case that $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to 0^+$.  Now, from the Osgood argument \eqref{Final Osgood Estimate} we have that 
$$
\int_{C_2(\left\lVertu_0\right\rVert_{L^\infty},\left\lVert\omega_0\right\rVert_{Y^{\theta}_{ul}},T)T\nu}^{Y(t)} \frac{ds}{C_3\beta_{M,\psi}(s)} \leq T,
$$
which in particular implies that $Y(t) \leq f(C_2(\left\lVertu_0\right\rVert_{L^\infty},\left\lVert\omega_0\right\rVert_{Y^{\theta}_{ul}},T)T\nu)$ so that 
\begin{equation}
\label{rate of convergence}
\left\lVert\overline{u}(t)\right\rVert_{L^2_{ul}} \leq \left(e^{\int_0^t C_1(s)ds}f\left(C_2(\left\lVertu_0\right\rVert_{L^\infty},\left\lVert\omega_0\right\rVert_{Y^{\theta}_{ul}},T)T\nu\right)\right)^\frac{1}{2}.
\end{equation}
